aliases: law of sines on the sphere
Book of Unknown Arcs of a Sphere

milestones.label: Menelaus' Sphaerica
milestones.work: Menelaus of Alexandria, Sphaerica (three books), c. 100 CE; Arabic versions edited by Rashed and Papadopoulos, 2017
milestones.description: The earliest surviving work on spherical triangles, with the rule of six quantities, which later Arabic authors rebuilt into a trigonometry of the sphere.

evidence.claim: Menelaus' surviving work on spherics is the earliest known work on spherical trigonometry (about 100 AD).
The Arabic versions of the Spherics (including the al-Mahani/al-Harawi version) were edited and translated in 2017.
evidence.source: Rashed, R. and Papadopoulos, A., Menelaus' Spherics, De Gruyter 2017 (Crossref record)

milestones.note: Precursor, not the Islamic start. Date is approximate (c. 100 CE).

milestones.label: Spherical law of sines in the circle of Abu'l-Wafa and Abu Nasr Mansur
milestones.work: No single dated work located; reported through al-Biruni's letters and al-Tusi's Shakl al-qatta'
milestones.description: The sine theorem for spherical triangles was found in the late tenth century; Abu'l-Wafa and Abu Nasr Mansur each claimed it and later authors credit al-Khujandi.

evidence.claim: Both Abu'l-Wafa and Abu Nasr Mansur claim the sine theorem; al-Tusi credits al-Khujandi with the proof for spherical triangles.
A letter of al-Biruni contains proofs of the plane and spherical sine theorem, attributed to his teacher Abu Nasr Mansur.

milestones.note: Priority is disputed and I found no dated primary record; year range is an inference from the lifespans (Abu'l-Wafa 940-998, al-Khujandi 940-1000). Left as a range, not a single year. No dated primary source for the spherical sine law; 970 is inferred from lifespans (MacTutor re-read in this pass: priority between Abu'l-Wafa, Abu Nasr Mansur and al-Khujandi unresolved).

milestones.label: Abu'l-Wafa: tangent function and sine/tangent tables
milestones.work: Abu'l-Wafa al-Buzjani, Theories of the Moon and Kitab al-Kamil (simplified Almagest)
milestones.description: Abu'l-Wafa is credited with the first use of the tangent and with sine and tangent tables at quarter-degree steps, giving the full set of functions needed for spherical work.

evidence.claim: Best known for the first use of the tan function and tables of sines and tangents at 15 minute steps; knew sin 2x = 2 sin x cos x by 980.
By 980 Abu'l-Wafa knew the double-angle identity.

milestones.note: Year 980 is MacTutor's marker for his knowledge of the identity, not a publication date.

milestones.label: Al-Jayyani, Book of Unknown Arcs of a Sphere
milestones.work: Ibn Mu'adh al-Jayyani, Kitab matahil al-qisi al-maghula 'ala al-kura (11th century)
milestones.description: A stand-alone treatise on spherical trigonometry in al-Andalus, with right-triangle rules, a general law of sines and the polar triangle.

evidence.claim: Described as the first treatise on spherical trigonometry; contains formulae for right triangles, the general law of sines and solution by the polar triangle.
al-Jayyani's computational work in 11th-century al-Andalus is studied by Hogendijk (2005).

milestones.note: No exact date found. al-Jayyani lived 989-after 1079; the range 1010-1079 is bounded only by his adult life. 'First treatise' is MacTutor's wording and competes with the claim for al-Tusi below.

milestones.label: Nasir al-Din al-Tusi, Treatise on the Quadrilateral
milestones.work: Nasir al-Din al-Tusi, Kitab shakl al-qatta' (Book on the complete quadrilateral), 13th century
milestones.description: The first extant exposition of plane and spherical trigonometry as a discipline apart from astronomy, listing all six right-triangle cases.

evidence.claim: In the Treatise on the Quadrilateral al-Tusi gave the first extant exposition of the whole system of plane and spherical trigonometry, as a discipline in its own right.
al-Tusi was the first to list the six distinct cases of a right spherical triangle.

milestones.note: Date not located in the sources read: he worked at the Maragheh observatory (begun 1259, died 1274). Treat 1250-1274 as a window. Composition year is not given by MacTutor or Wikipedia; the range shown is an estimate.

milestones.label: Regiomontanus, De triangulis omnimodis
milestones.work: Regiomontanus, De triangulis omnimodis (written 1464; printed 1533)
milestones.description: A systematic Latin account of solving triangles with books on spherical triangles, which carried the Islamic material into European use.

evidence.claim: De triangulis omnimodis (1464) is a systematic account of solving triangles; Books III-V treat spherical trigonometry.
One of Regiomontanus' sources is argued to be al-Jayyani's Book of Unknown Arcs.

milestones.note: 1464 is the date of writing; first printing is a later date I did not verify here.

works.citation: Sphaerica (three books)
works.whyItMatters: Earliest known work on spherical trigonometry; Arabic editions edited by Rashed and Papadopoulos.

works.citation: Kitab al-Kamil (simplified Almagest), tables of sines and tangents
works.whyItMatters: First use of the tangent function with tables; claimant of the sine theorem.

works.citation: De triangulis omnimodis
works.whyItMatters: Latin systematic treatise that brought triangle solving, including spherical, into European teaching.

notes: Summary says 'all six functions and sine laws': these come in stages over about 300 years, so priority claims are split across the phases. The sine law priority (Abu'l-Wafa, Abu Nasr Mansur, al-Khujandi) is disputed and has no dated primary record here. A Wikipedia sentence that Regiomontanus copied al-Tusi uncredited was not used: it is not supported by the MacTutor or bibliographic sources read. No MSC code or journal; naming/institution milestone not applicable (pre-modern). Van Brummelen 2009 (Princeton, Crossref 10.1515/9781400833313) and Berggren (Crossref 10.1007/978-1-4939-3780-6_6) are the modern surveys to consult for exact dates. person without verified work: Abu Mahmud al-Khujandi (developer). person without verified work: Ibn Mu'adh al-Jayyani (systematiser). person without verified work: Nasir al-Din al-Tusi (systematiser). Re-checked MacTutor Al-Khujandi in this pass: no dated work; Abu'l-Wafa or Abu Nasr Mansur is more likely than al-Khujandi as originator; the sine-law priority stays open.

canonicalName: Al-Mahani: geometric problems reduced to algebra
aliases: division of the sphere in a given ratio

milestones.label: Menaechmus: conics solve two mean proportionals
milestones.work: Menaechmus, solution of cube duplication by conic sections (as reported by Eutocius)
milestones.description: A cubic problem (doubling the cube) was solved by intersecting conics, the geometric tool later applied to cubic equations.

evidence.claim: Menaechmus found conic sections while trying to duplicate the cube, solving the two mean proportionals problem with them; described by Eutocius.

milestones.note: Approximate; lifespan 380-320 BCE.

milestones.label: Archimedes poses the sphere-section problem
milestones.work: Archimedes, On the Sphere and Cylinder II.4
milestones.description: Archimedes set the task of cutting a sphere by a plane so the pieces have a given volume ratio, and promised a solution later supplied by Eutocius' text.

evidence.claim: al-Mahani tried the Archimedes problem of cutting a sphere by a plane into segments of given volume ratio.
Eutocius records the missing solution promised by Archimedes in On the Sphere and Cylinder II.4.

milestones.note: Date approximate; Archimedes lived 287-212 BCE.

milestones.label: Al-Mahani reduces the sphere problem to a cubic
milestones.work: Al-Mahani, commentary on On the Sphere and Cylinder (lost); equation reported by Khayyam
milestones.description: He recast the Archimedean division of a sphere as an algebraic equation with cubes, squares and numbers, but could not solve it.

evidence.claim: al-Mahani reached an equation of cubes, squares and numbers he could not solve; Khayyam gives this account.
The resulting 'al-Mahani equation' is x^3 + c^2 b = c x^2, as reported by Khayyam.

milestones.note: His observations are dated 853-866 (Wikipedia, from Ibn Yunus), which supports flourishing c. 860; the algebraic work itself is undated and known only through Khayyam's report.

milestones.label: Al-Khazin solves al-Mahani's equation with conics
milestones.work: Abu Ja'far al-Khazin, solution of the sphere-division equation (10th century)
milestones.description: The equation was solved by intersecting conic sections, making the geometry-to-cubic link complete.

evidence.claim: The problem was declared impossible until Ja'far al-Khazin solved the equation with conic sections.
Khayyam credits al-Mahani and al-Khazin with translating geometric problems into algebraic ones.

milestones.note: al-Khazin lived 900-971; 'first' means first in the Arabic tradition here; Greek conic solutions of special problems (Menaechmus, Dionysodorus, Diocles) existed.

milestones.label: Khayyam classifies cubics solved by conics
milestones.work: Omar Khayyam, Treatise on Demonstration of Problems of Algebra (Samarkand, from 1070)
milestones.description: Khayyam gave a systematic classification of cubic equations with conic solutions, citing al-Mahani and al-Khazin as the starting point.

evidence.claim: Khayyam's Treatise gave a complete classification of cubics with solutions by intersecting conics and describes al-Mahani and al-Khazin.

milestones.note: Treatise written after his move to Samarkand in 1070 (MacTutor); he moved to Isfahan after 1073.

works.citation: Treatise on Demonstration of Problems of Algebra
works.whyItMatters: Reports al-Mahani's work and generalises it; Woepcke 1851 edition record.

works.citation: Netz, The Archimedes Codex (2007)
works.whyItMatters: Reconstructs the palimpsest that preserves Archimedes' Method, the source of his mechanical procedure.

notes: The event is the reduction (geometry to cubic equation); the conic solution is al-Khazin's, and the full theory is Khayyam's (see event P136). The date for al-Mahani's reduction is not on any dated work: only his observation years 853-866 and death c. 880 are recorded. Rashed and Papadopoulos 2017 (Crossref 10.1515/9783110571424) edit al-Mahani's version of Menelaus' Spherics, which confirms his work on Greek texts but not this equation. A bibliographic record for the equation itself (Rashed/Vahabzadeh 1999 on Khayyam, zbMATH 1419157) was found but not read in full. person without verified work: al-Mahani (Muhammad ibn Isa) (originator). person without verified work: Abu Ja'far al-Khazin (developer). person without verified work: Menaechmus (originator).

canonicalName: Ibn al-Haytham and Ibn Sinan: quadrature
aliases: quadrature of the parabola in Islam
Banu Musa Thabit Ibn Sinan Ibn al-Haytham quadrature

milestones.label: Archimedes' Quadrature of the Parabola
milestones.work: Archimedes, Quadrature of the Parabola
milestones.description: Found the area of a parabola segment by exhaustion, the Greek model for later Arabic work.

evidence.claim: In the Quadrature of the Parabola Archimedes finds the area of a segment cut off by any chord.
Overview of the work and its exhaustion proof.
evidence.source: English Wikipedia, Quadrature of the Parabola

milestones.note: Date approximate (Archimedes 287-212 BCE).

milestones.label: Thabit ibn Qurra: parabola and paraboloid by integral sums
milestones.work: Thabit ibn Qurra, treatises on the measurement of the parabola and paraboloid
milestones.description: Computed parabola and paraboloid measures using upper and lower sums with unequal subdivisions, apparently without Archimedes' own treatises.

evidence.claim: Thabit effectively integrated sqrt(x) using upper and lower integral sums and exhaustion, dividing the interval into unequal parts.

milestones.note: Dates are inferred from lifespan (836-901). 'First' within the Arabic tradition only; his method differs from the sums-of-powers method.

milestones.label: Ibrahim ibn Sinan: simpler parabola quadrature
milestones.work: Ibrahim ibn Sinan, Quadrature of the parabola (10th century)
milestones.description: He gave a shorter proof of the parabola's quadrature, generalising Archimedes without having his text.

evidence.claim: Ibrahim ibn Sinan advanced the quadrature of the parabola and integration theory, generalising Archimedes' work.
Ibrahim ibn Sinan lived c. 908-946 according to the Biographical Encyclopedia of Astronomers entry
evidence.source: Van Brummelen entry, Biographical Encyclopedia of Astronomers

milestones.note: He lived c. 908-946 (Wikipedia); the work is undated. Source cites Van Brummelen 2007, p. 574; I could not open that source. Dated only by the author's lifespan (c. 908-946); no source dates the quadrature, so 925 is a midpoint, not a dated fact.

milestones.label: Ibn al-Haytham: sum of fourth powers and paraboloid volume
milestones.work: Ibn al-Haytham, On the measurement of the paraboloid (early 11th century); studied by Rashed in Les mathematiques infinitesimales, vol. 2 (1993)
milestones.description: Derived a formula for the sum of fourth powers and used sums of powers to compute the volume of a paraboloid.

evidence.claim: Alhazen derived the sum of fourth powers, used it for the paraboloid volume, and could have generalised to higher powers.
Modern edition and study of Ibn al-Haytham's infinitesimal mathematics, volume 2, first published 1993.
evidence.source: Open Library: Rashed, Les mathematiques infinitesimales du IXe au XIe siecle

evidence.claim: MacTutor lists Rashed, 'Ibn al-Haytham and the measurement of the paraboloid', J. Hist. Arabic Sci. 5 (1981).

milestones.note: Exact date of the treatise unknown; he lived 965-1039. Marked first_application as the earliest use of power sums on volume; Thabit's earlier integral sums use another method.

milestones.label: Rashed's Les mathematiques infinitesimales
milestones.work: Roshdi Rashed, Les mathematiques infinitesimales du IXe au XIe siecle, vol. 2, 1993
milestones.description: Monograph on Arabic infinitesimal mathematics of the ninth to eleventh centuries, covering the quadrature work discussed in this event.

evidence.claim: Open Library record of Rashed's 1993 monograph.

milestones.note: Same book as the existing Ibn al-Haytham citation, given the consolidation role because it is the systematic treatment; the volume number comes from the existing record.

works.citation: Netz, The Archimedes Codex (2007)
works.whyItMatters: Reconstructs the palimpsest that preserves Archimedes' Method, the source of his mechanical procedure.

works.citation: Les mathematiques infinitesimales du IXe au XIe siecle, vol. 2 (Ibn al-Haytham)
works.whyItMatters: Modern edition; read by Celeyrette 1998 review in zbMATH 1300712.

works.citation: Roshdi Rashed, Les mathématiques infinitésimales du IXe au XIe siècle (Al-Furqan, 1993); the record places Ibn al-Haytham's paraboloid measurement in vol. 2
works.whyItMatters: Rashed's study of early-medieval quadrature, which the record uses for Ibn al-Haytham's sums of fourth powers and the paraboloid volume.

notes: Summary says 'sums of powers for areas and volumes' bundles three methods: Thabit's unequal sums, Ibn Sinan's quadrature, Ibn al-Haytham's power sums. MacTutor's Ibn al-Haytham page lists but does not describe the paraboloid work, so the key detail comes from Wikipedia plus Rashed's bibliographic record; I did not read Rashed. Banu Musa (9th c.) are likely earlier contributors but no source here confirmed their role. The step from here to calculus (Cavalieri, Fermat) was not researched. No institutional milestone. person without verified work: Thabit ibn Qurra (originator). person without verified work: Ibrahim ibn Sinan (developer). person without verified work: Ibn al-Haytham (developer).

canonicalName: Islamic work on the parallel postulate
aliases: la theorie des paralleles en pays d'Islam

milestones.label: Euclid's fifth postulate
milestones.work: Euclid, Elements, Book I, postulate 5
milestones.description: Euclid's parallel postulate, which later commentators tried to derive from the other postulates.

evidence.claim: The fourth and fifth postulates are of a different nature from the first three.
History of attempted proofs from Proclus on.

milestones.label: Thabit ibn Qurra on the parallels postulate
milestones.work: Thabit ibn Qurra, treatise on the parallels postulate; study by Sabra, J. Warburg & Courtauld Inst. 31 (1968)
milestones.description: One of the earliest Arabic attempts to prove the parallel postulate, using motion in geometry.

evidence.claim: Sabra's article studies Thabit ibn Qurra's treatment of Euclid's parallels postulate.

milestones.note: I did not find a source that says this is the first Arabic attempt, and earlier ones are possible (Jaouiche 1986, Rosenfeld 1988 not read). Range from his lifespan 836-901.

milestones.label: Ibn al-Haytham's attempted proof
milestones.work: Ibn al-Haytham, commentary on Euclid's premises (c. 1000)
milestones.description: He tried a proof by contradiction, characterising parallels as equidistant lines and using the quadrilateral later named for him and Lambert.

evidence.claim: Alhazen tried to prove the postulate by contradiction, introducing motion, and formulated the Lambert quadrilateral.

milestones.note: Date inferred from lifespan 965-1039.

milestones.label: Khayyam: Discussion of difficulties in Euclid's postulates
milestones.work: Omar Khayyam, Explanations of the Difficulties in the Postulates of Euclid (late 11th century)
milestones.description: Khayyam based the parallel postulate on a different postulate and studied the quadrilateral with two right base angles, reaching results of hyperbolic and elliptic geometry without seeing it.

evidence.claim: In Commentaries on the difficult postulates of Euclid he accidentally proved properties of figures in non-Euclidean geometries.
Saccheri quadrilateral first considered by Khayyam in the late 11th century.

milestones.note: Wikipedia gives lifespan 1050-1123, MacTutor 1048-1131.

milestones.label: Nasir al-Din al-Tusi: Discussion which removes doubt about parallel lines
milestones.work: Nasir al-Din al-Tusi, al-Risala al-shafiya 'an al-shakk fi'l-khutut al-mutawaziya (1250)
milestones.description: Critiqued Khayyam's attempt and tried his own proof by contradiction on the acute and obtuse cases.

evidence.claim: Al-Tusi's text, dated 1250, critiques Khayyam's attempted proof.

milestones.note: Date from Wikipedia only; not confirmed in a bibliographic record.

milestones.label: Arabic Euclid with al-Tusi's version printed in Rome
milestones.work: Arabic edition of the Elements, Rome, 1594
milestones.description: The printed edition reached European geometers and led Wallis and Saccheri to the problem.

evidence.claim: Work published in Rome in 1594 and studied by European geometers; start of Saccheri's work.

milestones.note: Wikipedia attributes the revision to Sadr al-Din (al-Tusi's son); not checked elsewhere.

milestones.label: Saccheri, Euclides ab omni naevo vindicatus
milestones.work: Girolamo Saccheri, Euclides ab omni naevo vindicatus, Milan 1733
milestones.description: Saccheri assumed the postulate false and derived consequences of non-Euclidean geometry while trying to refute it, in the same quadrilateral tradition.

evidence.claim: Euclides ab omni naevo vindicatus was published in 1733.
Saccheri assumed the fifth postulate false hoping to reach a contradiction.

works.citation: Treatise on the parallels postulate (study: Sabra 1968)
works.whyItMatters: Earliest treatment in my sources.

works.citation: Discussion Which Removes Doubt about Parallel Lines
works.whyItMatters: Critique of Khayyam and own attempt.

works.citation: Euclides ab omni naevo vindicatus
works.whyItMatters: European continuation.

works.citation: Attempted proof of the fifth postulate
works.whyItMatters: Proof based on the existence of similar triangles; Wikipedia says he translated al-Tusi's commentary.

notes: Dates for Islamic works are approximate; Jaouiche 1986 and Rosenfeld 1988 (reviewed in Crossref: De Young 1990 10.1086/355388, Gray 1991 10.1016/0315-0860(91)90380-g) are the standard modern accounts and were not read. The chain from Tusi to Wallis and Saccheri is a claim in Wikipedia and is not independently confirmed. Naming or institution: none, 'non-Euclidean geometry' belongs to the nineteenth century. person without verified work: Ibn al-Haytham (developer). person without verified work: Omar Khayyam (developer).

canonicalName: Al-Karaji: binomial coefficients and early induction

milestones.label: Pingala's Meruprastara
milestones.work: Pingala, Chandahshastra
milestones.description: A triangular array counting poetic metres, later read as the binomial coefficient triangle.

evidence.claim: Pingala (3rd or 2nd century BCE) arranged counts in a form later read as Pascal's triangle.

milestones.note: Whether this is a binomial triangle is itself debated; included only as an Indian precursor.

milestones.label: Al-Karaji: binomial coefficients and stepwise argument
milestones.work: Al-Karaji, Al-Fakhri and Al-Badi' (c. 1000); quoted by al-Samaw'al
milestones.description: Built the triangle of binomial coefficients and gave arguments that move from case n to n+1, an early form of induction.

evidence.claim: Al-Karaji used a form of induction in his work on the binomial theorem and the Pascal triangle; (a+b)^3 in Al-Fakhri, (a+b)^4 in Al-Badi'.
Rashed's 1972 study identifies mathematical induction in al-Karaji and al-Samaw'al.
evidence.source: zbMATH 3410980, Rashed, Arch. Hist. Exact Sci. 9 (1972) 1-21

milestones.note: The original is lost and known only through al-Samaw'al. Date inferred from 953-1029 and from Al-Fakhri being written in Baghdad.

milestones.label: Al-Samaw'al: al-Bahir fi'l-jabr
milestones.work: Al-Samaw'al, al-Bahir fi'l-jabr (written at 19)
milestones.description: Preserved al-Karaji's triangle and used the same recursive reasoning for sums and the binomial theorem.

evidence.claim: al-Bahir written at nineteen; records lost works of al-Karaji; gives the binomial theorem with Pascal triangle coefficients and an early form of induction.
al-Samaw'al extended results to n=12.

milestones.note: Year derived from birth c. 1130 plus age 19; Wikipedia's induction page says c. 1150.

milestones.label: Maurolico: early printed explicit induction proof
milestones.work: Francesco Maurolico, Arithmeticorum libri duo (written 1557, printed 1575)
milestones.description: Used an induction step to prove that the first n odd numbers sum to n squared.

evidence.claim: Arithmeticorum libri duo, written in 1557 and published with Opuscula Mathematica, contains a proof by induction claimed to be the first genuine one.
Maurolico used the technique in 1575.
Wikipedia: earliest rigorous use of induction is by Gersonides (1288-1344); Maurolico (1575) is cited as a separate case

milestones.note: The 'first' claim is disputed in the literature quoted by MacTutor and Wikipedia. The label was softened from "first": Wikipedia credits Gersonides with the earliest rigorous use.

milestones.label: Pascal, Traite du triangle arithmetique
milestones.work: Blaise Pascal, Traite du triangle arithmetique (written 1654; published 1665)
milestones.description: The first systematic treatise on the triangle, with an explicit induction principle.

evidence.claim: Open Library record, first publication 1665.
evidence.source: Open Library: Pascal, Traite du triangle arithmetique

evidence.claim: Pascal was not the first to study the triangle, but his Treatise was the most important work on it.
Pascal gave the first explicit formulation of the induction principle in the Traite (1665).

milestones.note: Publication year governs (posthumous).

works.citation: Arithmeticorum libri duo
works.whyItMatters: Explicit induction step in Europe.

works.citation: Traite du triangle arithmetique
works.whyItMatters: Systematic treatment of the triangle and induction.

works.citation: L'induction mathematique: al-Karaji, as-Samaw'al
works.whyItMatters: Modern historian who identified the induction in these texts.

works.citation: Al-Karaji (Karaji), Al-Fakhri (original c. 1010, approximate); extract edited and translated by Franz Woepcke, Paris, 1853
works.whyItMatters: 19th-century edition of part of al-Karaji's algebra treatise Al-Fakhri, the main surviving source (per MacTutor) for his arithmetised polynomial algebra.

works.citation: Al-Samaw'al, al-Bahir fi'l-jabr (written c. 1149, at about nineteen per MacTutor); edition 'Al-Bahir en algèbre d'As-Samaw'al' (Damascus, 1972)
works.whyItMatters: The record credits this algebra treatise with carrying al-Karaji's binomial arguments forward; the passage was not read here.

notes: The summary is accurate but 'early induction' is a modern reading: the arguments run up to n of about 5 and then say 'continue', so MacTutor calls them not induction proper. The Chinese triangle (Jia Xian) is a separate, probably independent track, see P155. Karaji's date is not on any dated work. No naming or institution milestone applies. person without verified work: Al-Karaji (originator). person without verified work: Al-Samaw'al (developer).

milestones.label: Al-Khwarizmi's Algebra
milestones.work: Al-Khwarizmi, Kitab al-jabr wa'l-muqabala (c. 820)
milestones.description: Gave the six standard equation types with solutions by rules and by geometric completion of the square, with no polynomial calculus.

evidence.claim: Shows how to solve six standard types of equation using algebraic and geometric methods, e.g. completing the square.

milestones.note: Date inferred from his lifespan; the work is placed at the start of the ninth century.

milestones.label: Abu Kamil's Book on Algebra
milestones.work: Abu Kamil, Book on algebra (c. 900)
milestones.description: Extended al-Khwarizmi's methods and applied algebra to geometric problems.

evidence.claim: Abu Kamil was a successor of al-Khwarizmi who applied algebraic methods to geometric problems; his Book on algebra survives.

milestones.note: Lifespan c. 850-930; date of the book is not given.

milestones.label: Al-Karaji, Al-Fakhri: monomials and polynomial arithmetic
milestones.work: Al-Karaji, Al-Fakhri fi'l-jabr wa'l-muqabala
milestones.description: Defined the powers x^n and 1/x^n as monomials and gave multiplication of polynomials, freeing algebra from geometric operations.

evidence.claim: What al-Karaji achieved in Al-Fakhri was first to define the monomials x, x^2, x^3, ... and 1/x, 1/x^2, ...
His work gave rules for adding, subtracting and multiplying polynomials, though division was only by monomials.

milestones.note: Al-Fakhri was written in Baghdad before he left the city; no firmer date was found.

milestones.label: Al-Samaw'al, al-Bahir fi'l-jabr
milestones.work: Al-Samaw'al, al-Bahir fi'l-jabr (written at 19)
milestones.description: Treated polynomial arithmetic more fully, including division and root extraction, and defined powers with negative exponents.

evidence.claim: Al-Samawal extended arithmetic to polynomials; in Book 1 he defines x, x^2, ..., x^-1, x^-2 and the study resembles polynomial rings.

milestones.note: Year derived from birth c. 1130 plus age 19.

milestones.label: Woepcke's extract of al-Karaji's al-Fakhri
milestones.work: Franz Woepcke, Extrait du Fakhri, Paris, 1853
milestones.description: French extract of al-Karaji's algebra, the first printed exposition of his polynomial arithmetic available to European readers.

evidence.claim: Open Library record of Woepcke's 1853 Extrait du Fakhri.
Woepcke was the first historian to realise the importance of al-Karaji's work.

milestones.note: Relies on the Wikipedia statement about Woepcke; the 'first printed exposition' wording is my summary and was not checked against the text itself.

works.citation: Rosen, The Algebra of Mohammed ben Musa (1831; Cambridge reprint, 2013)
works.whyItMatters: Standard English translation of al-Khwarizmi's algebra, which al-Karaji's work moved beyond.

works.citation: Abu Kamil, The Algebra of Abu Kamil, with a commentary by Mordecai Finkelstein (1967)
works.whyItMatters: Edition and commentary on Abu Kamil's algebra, which extends al-Khwarizmi's methods.

works.citation: Entre arithmetique et algebre
works.whyItMatters: Modern account of this school; reviewed in Isis 1990 (Crossref 10.1086/355389).

works.citation: Al-Karaji (Karaji), Al-Fakhri (original c. 1010, approximate); extract edited and translated by Franz Woepcke, Paris, 1853
works.whyItMatters: 19th-century edition of part of al-Karaji's algebra treatise Al-Fakhri, the main surviving source (per MacTutor) for his arithmetised polynomial algebra.

works.citation: Al-Samaw'al, al-Bahir fi'l-jabr (written c. 1149, at about nineteen per MacTutor); edition 'Al-Bahir en algèbre d'As-Samaw'al' (Damascus, 1972)
works.whyItMatters: MacTutor states that the first book of al-Bahir defines the powers x, x^2, x^3, which is the polynomial-algebra step the record dates here.

notes: The wording 'freed from geometry' is MacTutor's, and MacTutor also quotes a more critical modern view (Berggren-style) that al-Karaji often still justifies by pictures. Neither a dated manuscript nor a naming/institution milestone was found; the word 'algebra' itself belongs to al-Khwarizmi's title (c. 820) and is not a milestone of this event. The relation to P177 (induction) is the same lost text, so milestones overlap on al-Samaw'al. person without verified work: Al-Karaji (originator). person without verified work: Al-Samaw'al (developer).

canonicalName: Numerical solution of polynomial equations in China (Ruffini-Horner)

milestones.label: Wang Xiaotong: numerical solution of cubics
milestones.work: Wang Xiaotong, Jigu suanjing (written before 626)
milestones.description: The first known Chinese treatment of cubic equations, solved numerically by extending the cube-root algorithm.

evidence.claim: The problems reduce to cubic equations which Wang solves numerically; no earlier Chinese work on cubics is known.
Jigu suanjing was written before the year 626.

milestones.note: Window 620-626 starts from his 623 calendar assignment; the exact year is unknown.

milestones.label: Jia Xian: additive-multiplicative root method for any degree
milestones.work: Jia Xian, Shi suo suan shu (lost), reported by Yang Hui, 1261
milestones.description: Generalised root extraction to nth roots and polynomial equations using binomial coefficients from his triangle; essentially the Ruffini-Horner scheme.

evidence.claim: The Zeng cheng kaifang method for roots and polynomial equations is essentially the Ruffini-Horner method.

milestones.note: Lost book; date inferred from his teacher Chu Yan's activity 1022-1054. Known only from Yang Hui.

milestones.label: Qin Jiushao: equations up to degree 10
milestones.work: Qin Jiushao, Shushu jiuzhang (Mathematical Treatise in Nine Sections), 1247
milestones.description: Applied the scheme to cubic, quartic and a tenth-degree equation in worked problems.

evidence.claim: Shushu jiuzhang appeared in 1247 and solves cubics and quartics by the Ruffini-Horner method.
Treatise covers numerical solution up to the tenth degree.
Libbrecht's 1973 study of Qin's Shu-shu chiu-chang.

milestones.label: Zhu Shijie: transformation method to degree 14
milestones.work: Zhu Shijie, Siyuan yujian (Jade Mirror of the Four Unknowns), 1303
milestones.description: Gave a transformation method for numerical solution of equations up to degree 14, based on the same scheme.

evidence.claim: Contains a transformation method for equations up to degree 14, based on the method rediscovered by Horner and Ruffini.

milestones.label: Ruffini's method
milestones.work: Paolo Ruffini, memoir awarded 1804, with refinements 1807 and 1813
milestones.description: In Europe, Ruffini gave a rule equivalent to the method; it won a prize and was published in 1804.

evidence.claim: Ruffini's method was awarded first place and published in 1804, with refinements in 1807 and 1813.
Cajori argues that Horner's method was anticipated by Ruffini.

milestones.note: Wikipedia's Horner article dates Ruffini's rule to 1809; the 1804 date is from the Ruffini's rule article.

milestones.label: Horner, A new method of solving numerical equations
milestones.work: W. G. Horner, Phil. Trans. R. Soc. 109 (1819)
milestones.description: The English paper that gave the method its name in the West.

evidence.claim: Crossref record of the paper.
MacTutor reports that Fuller found the 1819 article does not contain the method, and that one published by Horner in 1830 does.

milestones.note: Dispute: Wikipedia says the method is described in 1819; MacTutor (citing Fuller 1999, Crossref 10.1006/hmat.1998.2214) says 1830. Left unresolved.

milestones.label: Libbrecht's monograph on thirteenth-century Chinese mathematics
milestones.work: Ulrich Libbrecht, Chinese Mathematics in the Thirteenth Century, MIT Press, 1973
milestones.description: Monograph on the thirteenth-century Chinese mathematics in which the numerical equation methods of Qin Jiushao and Zhu Shijie are set out.

evidence.claim: Open Library record of Libbrecht's 1973 monograph on thirteenth-century Chinese mathematics.

milestones.note: Content claim about Qin and Zhu comes from the subject of the book, not from a checked table of contents.

milestones.label: Square and cube roots in the Nine Chapters
milestones.work: Jiuzhang suanshu (Nine Chapters on the Mathematical Art), root-extraction problems
milestones.description: The classical Chinese algorithms for square and cube roots, which later authors generalised.

evidence.claim: Chapter 4 problems extract square and cube roots; the Han-era text was commented on by Liu Hui in 263.
Wikipedia lists the Nine Chapters among the sources where Horner's method was already known.

milestones.note: No firm date for the root algorithms; the text is of the Han period (202 BCE-220 CE) with Liu Hui's commentary of 263. Year left null as a precursor.

works.citation: Jigu suanjing
works.whyItMatters: First Chinese cubic equations.

works.citation: Shushu jiuzhang
works.whyItMatters: Worked examples to degree 10; Libbrecht 1973 study.

works.citation: Siyuan yujian
works.whyItMatters: Higher-degree transformation method.

works.citation: Memoir on numerical roots of equations
works.whyItMatters: European anticipation; see Cajori 1911.

works.citation: A new method of solving numerical equations of all orders, by continuous approximation
works.whyItMatters: Gave the name; priority disputed.

notes: Chemla 1994 (Crossref 10.1017/s0957423900001235) compares Chinese and Arabic root extraction; Lam 1980 (Crossref 10.1016/0315-0860(80)90005-1) links the Pascal triangle to the equation solving. Neither was read in full. No dated Arabic or Indian precedent is included; al-Samaw'al and Sharaf al-Din al-Tusi are sometimes named. The summary says 'extended step by step', which fits Wang, Jia, Qin, Zhu. No naming or institution milestone: the label 'Ruffini-Horner' arises in the nineteenth century (De Morgan, per MacTutor) with no date found. person without verified work: Jia Xian (developer).

aliases: table of the ancient method of powers

milestones.label: Pingala's Meruprastara
milestones.work: Pingala, Chandahshastra
milestones.description: A counting array for metres later read as binomial coefficients.

evidence.claim: Pingala (3rd/2nd century BCE) arranged counts of metres in a form later called Pascal's triangle.

milestones.note: Indian precedent, unconnected to China; reading as binomial triangle is debated.

milestones.label: Halayudha's commentary on Pingala
milestones.work: Halayudha, Mritasanjivani, c. 975
milestones.description: Described the Meruprastara as the arithmetic triangle.

evidence.claim: Halayudha (c. 975) clearly described the Meruprastara as what is now known as the arithmetic triangle.

milestones.label: Jia Xian's table of binomial coefficients
milestones.work: Jia Xian, Shi suo suan shu (lost)
milestones.description: A table of coefficients of (a+b)^n up to n=6, built by adding the two entries above, used for root extraction.

evidence.claim: Jia Xian gave a table of binomial coefficients like Pascal's triangle up to row 1 6 15 20 15 6 1 and understood the additive generation rule.
Jia Xian described Pascal's triangle in the 11th century and used it for extracting roots.

milestones.note: Lost work; date from his teacher Chu Yan's activity 1022-1054.

milestones.label: Yang Hui, Xiangjie jiuzhang suanfa
milestones.work: Yang Hui, Xiangjie jiuzhang suanfa (1261)
milestones.description: The surviving source for the triangle, up to the sixth row, attributed to Jia Xian.

evidence.claim: In 1261 Yang wrote the Detailed analysis; he gives the triangle up to the sixth row, saying he learnt it from Jia Xian's treatise.

milestones.note: Earliest surviving Chinese record.

milestones.label: Zhu Shijie's diagram to the eighth power
milestones.work: Zhu Shijie, Siyuan yujian (1303)
milestones.description: The diagram gives coefficients up to the eighth power, called the 'ancient method' table.

evidence.claim: The book opens with Pascal's triangle giving coefficients up to the eighth power; Zhu makes no claim of originality.

milestones.label: Pascal, Traite du triangle arithmetique
milestones.work: Blaise Pascal, Traite du triangle arithmetique (1665)
milestones.description: The first systematic treatise on the triangle in Europe, with applications to probability.

evidence.claim: Open Library record, first published 1665.
Pascal collected known results and used them in probability, published posthumously in 1665.

milestones.label: Montmort names it for Pascal
milestones.work: Pierre Raymond de Montmort (1708)
milestones.description: The European name 'Pascal's triangle' dates from Montmort's 'table de M. Pascal'.

evidence.claim: Triangle later named for Pascal by Montmort (1708).

milestones.note: Chinese tradition names it for Yang Hui.

works.citation: Xiangjie jiuzhang suanfa
works.whyItMatters: Surviving record.

works.citation: Siyuan yujian
works.whyItMatters: Picture of the triangle to the eighth power.

works.citation: Traite du triangle arithmetique
works.whyItMatters: European systematic treatment.

works.citation: The Chinese connection between the Pascal triangle and the solution of numerical equations of any degree
works.whyItMatters: Historia Mathematica 7: links triangle and equation solving.

notes: Summary says 'up to the eighth power' is Zhu Shijie (1303), while the earliest record is only to the sixth row (Yang Hui 1261, from Jia Xian c. 1050). Jia Xian is lost; dates come from Yang. Whether Chinese, Indian and Arabic triangles are independent is not settled. No MSC-era naming milestone. person without verified work: Jia Xian (originator).

aliases: Treatise on Demonstration of Problems of Algebra

milestones.label: Menaechmus: conics for the cube
milestones.work: Menaechmus, solution of two mean proportionals by conics
milestones.description: Conic sections used to solve a cubic problem of geometry.

evidence.claim: Menaechmus discovered conic sections while duplicating the cube and solved it with them (reported by Eutocius).

milestones.label: Eutocius' commentary collects conic solutions
milestones.work: Eutocius, commentary on Archimedes' On the Sphere and Cylinder
milestones.description: Preserved earlier solutions of the cube-doubling problem, including those by conics, and the solution promised by Archimedes.

evidence.claim: Eutocius's commentary records several solutions of cube duplication (Menaechmus, Diocles and others) and the solution promised by Archimedes.

milestones.note: First commentary on Archimedes written c. 510 per MacTutor.

milestones.label: Al-Mahani's equation
milestones.work: Al-Mahani, reduction of Archimedes' sphere problem to a cubic
milestones.description: Turned a geometric problem into a cubic equation, which he could not solve.

evidence.claim: Khayyam notes that al-Mahani and al-Khazin translated geometric problems into algebraic ones.
al-Mahani reached an equation with cubes, squares and numbers.

milestones.note: See P160.

milestones.label: Al-Khazin solves it with conics
milestones.work: Abu Ja'far al-Khazin, solution by conic sections (10th century)
milestones.description: First recorded conic solution of a cubic equation in Arabic.

evidence.claim: al-Khazin solved the equation with the help of conic sections.

milestones.note: Lifespan 900-971; date range not documented. Reclassified from first_application to precursor: it predates this event's first statement (1070) and belongs to the wider field.

milestones.label: Khayyam, Treatise on Demonstration of Problems of Algebra
milestones.work: Omar Khayyam, Treatise on Demonstration of Problems of Algebra (Samarkand)
milestones.description: A classification of cubic types with geometric solutions by intersecting conics, with the claim that ruler and compass cannot suffice.

evidence.claim: Contains a complete classification of cubic equations with geometric solutions found by intersecting conic sections; states ruler and compass cannot solve them.
Khayyam gave a general solution of third-degree equations by intersecting two conics.

milestones.note: Written after his move to Samarkand in 1070 (MacTutor).

milestones.label: Sharaf al-Din al-Tusi analyses roots of cubics
milestones.work: Sharaf al-Din al-Tusi, Treatise on equations
milestones.description: Pursued the same cubic types algebraically, using maxima of polynomials to decide existence of roots.

evidence.claim: He divides equations of degree at most three into 25 types and studies roots through maxima.

milestones.note: Undated: window from c. 1165, when he taught in Damascus, to death in 1213.

milestones.label: Descartes, La Geometrie
milestones.work: Rene Descartes, La Geometrie (Leiden, 1637)
milestones.description: The geometric treatment of cubics by intersection of curves is compared with Khayyam's, often credited to Descartes.

evidence.claim: La Geometrie was published at Leiden in 1637.
Khayyam's two-conic method is often later attributed to Descartes.

milestones.note: No direct line from Khayyam to Descartes is shown in the sources read.

milestones.label: Woepcke's French edition of Khayyam's algebra
milestones.work: Franz Woepcke, L'algebre d'Omar Alkhayyami, Paris, 1851
milestones.description: French edition and translation of Khayyam's algebra, which contains his cubic-by-conics method, made available to European readers.

evidence.claim: Open Library record of the 1851 edition and translation by Woepcke.
Khayyam's algebra is described as the first systematic study of cubic equations, and Woepcke's 1851 translation is credited.

works.citation: Treatise on Demonstration of Problems of Algebra
works.whyItMatters: Open Library record for Woepcke's 1851 edition.

works.citation: L'Algebre d'Omar Alkhayyami
works.whyItMatters: Edition and French translation (Open Library record).

works.citation: Al-Khayyam the mathematician (with B. Vahabzadeh)
works.whyItMatters: Modern edition; review record Cooper 2003 in JAOS.

notes: 'Precursor of algebraic geometry' in the summary is a historiographic claim: Rashed says so for Sharaf al-Din; Oaks disputes it (Wikipedia, Sharaf al-Din al-Tusi), arguing both Khayyam and Sharaf study equations by curves, not curves by equations. MacTutor says the impossibility by ruler and compass was proved about 750 years later. MacTutor gives Khayyam 1048-1131 (18 May 1048 to 4 December 1131), and the Wikipedia infobox agrees, so the earlier 1050-1123 discrepancy no longer stands. Descartes' priority is not claimed. Not verified: Woepcke 1851 content beyond the Open Library record. person without verified work: al-Mahani (developer). person without verified work: Abu Ja'far al-Khazin (developer). person without verified work: Menaechmus (originator).

aliases: discriminant of the cubic in Islamic mathematics

milestones.label: Khayyam's conic treatment of cubics
milestones.work: Omar Khayyam, Treatise on Demonstration of Problems of Algebra
milestones.description: Geometric classification of cubics that Sharaf al-Din's algebraic approach contrasts with.

evidence.claim: Khayyam's treatise classified cubics with conic solutions.

milestones.label: Sharaf al-Din al-Tusi, Treatise on equations
milestones.work: Sharaf al-Din al-Tusi, al-Mu'adalat (Treatise on equations)
milestones.description: Treated 25 types of equation of degree at most three and decided the existence of positive roots of cubics through maxima of the polynomial.

evidence.claim: Equations of degree at most three divided into 25 types; maximum of bx - x^3 found at x = sqrt(b/3), giving a discriminant condition.
He gave the maximum of the cubic for five types and concluded the number of positive solutions.
Hogendijk analyses how Sharaf al-Din counts positive roots of cubics.

milestones.note: No date for the treatise found; window starts c. 1165 (Damascus, MacTutor) and ends at death in 1213.

milestones.label: Rashed's study linking Sharaf al-Din and Viete
milestones.work: Roshdi Rashed, Resolution des equations numeriques et algebre: Saraf-al-Din al-Tusi, Viete, Arch. Hist. Exact Sci. 12 (1974)
milestones.description: Modern recognition of the treatise's numerical method and its relation to later European algebra.
milestones.note: Historiographic milestone, not a development of the mathematics.

milestones.label: Hogendijk on positive roots of cubics
milestones.work: Jan P. Hogendijk, Hist. Math. 16 (1989) 69-85
milestones.description: Reassessment of what the treatise shows about roots and the discriminant.

evidence.claim: Hogendijk 1989.

works.citation: Treatise on Demonstration of Problems of Algebra
works.whyItMatters: Geometric classification before Sharaf.

works.citation: Resolution des equations numeriques et algebre
works.whyItMatters: Edited and interpreted the treatise.

works.citation: Sharaf al-Din al-Tusi on the number of positive roots of cubic equations
works.whyItMatters: Analysed his root counts.

works.citation: Sharaf al-Din al-Tusi, Treatise on equations (al-Mu'adalat; undated, late 12th century); edited in Roshdi Rashed (ed.), Œuvres mathématiques: Algèbre et géométrie au XIIe siècle (Les Belles Lettres, 1986)
works.whyItMatters: The edition contains the cubic-equation treatise that the record names as the originating work of Sharaf al-Din's approach to equations.

notes: Disputed: Rashed says the treatise opens algebraic geometry; Oaks (reported on Wikipedia) disagrees. Whether his maxima come from a derivative is disputed (MacTutor, Wikipedia). Treatise date is unknown. Houzel 1995 (zbMATH 851475) links his method to the Newton polygon and Fares 1995 (arXiv 0912.1130) discusses its analytic aspects; neither was read in detail. The 1986 Oeuvres mathematiques edition is mentioned in reviews (Crossref 10.1086/355109) but I did not confirm publisher or year. The summary's 'analysis-like extremum methods' matches MacTutor, not a claim of calculus. person without verified work: Sharaf al-Din al-Tusi (originator). person without verified work: Jeffrey Oaks (popularizer). Edition year (1986 or 1987) is still unconfirmed; the Rashed edition review in Isis (1989) was cited in the prior pass and not reopened here.
